sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI
Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: **Speech is a complex learned skill.** Children learn to coordinate their speech organs with little explicit instruction and very little visual feedback about what those organs are doing.
children: A child can develop a large vocabulary and near-adult language between about two and four years of age. Reading and writing whole words develop later and require much more explicit instruction.

teaching.text: **Articulatory phonetics** studies how structures in the vocal tract move to produce speech. The tongue and lips must make coordinated movements to produce different sounds.
**Speech technology** attempts to model this human ability. Understanding human speech and understanding how AI models speech are connected questions.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics** studies speech sounds, including how air vibrates in the vocal tract. The vocal tract is the air passage shaped by the tongue and the surrounding structures.
children: The air passage bends through the throat and mouth. The orange arrows connect that curved passage with a straightened representation of the same air space. **Straightening the model changes its geometry, not the material being studied.** The vibration concerns the air in that space.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: **AI literacy means understanding how AI systems operate.** Knowing how to build or use a system does not necessarily explain how its behavior arises.
AI has psychological, economic, social and environmental harms, as well as potential benefits in areas such as medicine and environmental engineering.
children: Understanding these systems helps people assess their benefits and harms. This matters for scientists using AI, politicians developing rules and lawyers dealing with its consequences.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: Understanding **human speech**, **basic physical principles** and **AI models of cognition** connects several kinds of knowledge. Speech can be studied as a cognitive skill, a physical process and a skill that a computer attempts to model.

**Elementary programming** develops methodical reasoning. Working across linguistics, physics, psychology, biology and computer science also develops the ability to connect ideas and use AI more thoughtfully.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima’s ladder** distinguishes memorization and repetition from creative understanding. **Creative reasoning** asks how ideas relate. Similar-looking things can work differently, and different-looking things can share an underlying principle.
children: Asking and answering questions develops this kind of understanding. It involves posing problems, solving them, reading critically and explaining ideas rather than only repeating them.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: **Voicing** means whether the vocal folds vibrate. The sounds in each pair keep the same place of articulation while changing voicing.
children: The pairs are f and v, th in “thing” and th in “that,” s and z, and sh in “mesh” and the sound in “beige.” The second sound in each pair is voiced.

teaching.text: **Place of articulation** identifies where the vocal tract is narrowed. Moving from one pair to another changes that location. Voicing and place therefore describe different properties of a consonant.

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: **Fricatives** are produced by sending air through a narrow opening. Their classification combines **place of articulation** with **voicing**.
children: **Labial** f and v use the lip region. **Dental** th sounds use the teeth. **Alveolar** s and z use the ridge just behind the upper teeth. **Postalveolar** sh and the sound in “beige” are produced farther back.

The **columns** change place of articulation from the lips toward the back of the mouth. The **rows** change voicing while keeping place fixed. The tongue and lip images under the columns identify the location of the narrowing.

teaching.text: Each place has a voiceless and a voiced member. For example, f and v share their place but differ in whether the vocal folds vibrate.
children: The label **j** represents the voiced fricative in “beige.” It belongs with sh in the postalveolar column. The two written **th** labels also represent different sounds, the voiceless sound in “thing” and the voiced sound in “that.”

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: A **stop** involves a complete closure in the mouth. The place of that closure distinguishes three groups.
children: The lips close for **p, b and m**. The tongue tip closes at the alveolar ridge for **t, d and n**. The back of the tongue closes at the velum, or soft palate, for **k, g and ng**.
The three **rows** group sounds by the location of the closure. The positions across a row compare a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop and a nasal stop at that same place.

teaching.text: Among the **oral stops**, p, t and k are voiceless, while b, d and g are voiced. Air is released through the mouth when the closure opens.
The **nasal stops** m, n and ng keep the mouth closed while air escapes through the nose. The **velum** lowers to open that route.
children: For example, d and n are both voiced and alveolar. Their difference is the oral or nasal route taken by the air.

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech
Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: **Fricatives** use a narrow opening in the vocal tract. The **place of articulation** identifies the location of that opening, while **voicing** identifies whether the vocal folds vibrate.
children: The labial pair is f and v. The dental pair is th in “thing” and th in “that.” The alveolar pair is s and z. The postalveolar pair is sh and the sound in “beige.”

Each **column** holds one place of articulation, and the two **rows** compare voiceless and voiced sounds. The MRI images identify where the narrowing is made. The label **j** refers to the voiced fricative in “beige.”

teaching.text: Within each pair, the place stays the same and voicing changes. Comparing f with s changes place instead.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: A **stop** has a complete closure in the mouth. The lips produce p, b and m. The tongue tip at the alveolar ridge produces t, d and n. The tongue back at the velum produces k, g and ng.
children: The rows group sounds by the location of the mouth closure. Across a row, the sounds keep that place while changing voicing or the route taken by the air.

teaching.text: **Oral stops** release the air through the mouth. The voiceless oral stops are p, t and k, and the voiced oral stops are b, d and g.
children: For **nasal stops**, the velum lowers so air can leave through the nose while the mouth stays closed. These are m, n and ng.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: Consonants are organized by **voicing**, **place of articulation** and **manner of articulation**. Voicing concerns vocal-fold vibration, place concerns where the mouth is narrowed or closed, and manner concerns how air passes through.
children: **Fricatives** allow air through a narrow gap. **Oral stops**, also called **plosives**, close the mouth passage and release air through it. **Nasal stops** close the mouth passage while letting air leave through the nose.

teaching.text: The **place columns** run from labial to velar, while the **manner groups** separate fricatives, oral stops and nasal stops. Within a manner group, the voice labels distinguish vocal-fold vibration.
children: For **d and n**, the alveolar column holds place fixed and the voiced labels hold voicing fixed. Moving between their manner groups changes the oral or nasal route of the air. The fricative label **j** means the sound in “beige.”
English nasal stops are voiced. Recognizing this organization shows how much structured knowledge is involved in producing ordinary consonants.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **Artificial intelligence, or AI, models psychological abilities** such as knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. These are abilities found in animals, including humans.
Ideas about human behavior and cognition contribute to AI design. AI therefore has connections to the study of minds and brains, as well as to computing.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: The **cloze procedure** tests completion. Words are removed from a passage, and a reader supplies the missing words.
children: The procedure was developed to measure readability. Completing a passage requires using the words that remain to work out what belongs in the gaps.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: **Closure** is the tendency to perceive a complete familiar pattern even when part of it is missing. The broken circular shapes support the perception of a whole shape that is not fully drawn.
The **cloze procedure** applies completion to language. A reader uses the surrounding words to supply a missing word.
children: Successful completion depends on knowledge of the language. The answer must fit the pattern formed by the available words.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: **Completion** can test knowledge by asking a system to supply a missing part of a sequence. A successful answer shows that the system can use the pattern in the available information.
This approach treats an AI system’s knowledge in terms of its ability to complete sequences. **Prediction** is another way to describe supplying the expected continuation.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT predicts the next word from the words supplied to it.** Each input word is represented by a **vector**, a list of numbers. The separate vertical strips represent the vectors for “chickens,” “cackle,” “and” and “ducks.”
children: Different words receive different vectors. The example **1,024 numbers** describes how many entries one input vector could contain. Those entries represent one word; they are not 1,024 possible next words.

teaching.text: The long output vector is a **probability distribution**. Its entries correspond to possible next words, such as “a,” “cat,” “quack” and “Zulu.”
children: The example **10,000 numbers** means one probability for each of 10,000 possible next words. For “chickens cackle and ducks,” **quack** should receive a high probability, while an unrelated continuation such as “cat” should receive a low probability.

teaching.text: **Input-vector entries and output probabilities have different roles.** The input represents words already supplied. The output assigns probabilities to candidate continuations.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: **Weights** are numbers that hold the system’s learned knowledge. The input vectors represent the words supplied to the system, and the weights help transform those inputs into predictions.
children: The vertical input strips are the **x’s**, representing the supplied words. The long output vector holds probabilities for candidate next words. The **pdf** label refers to that output distribution.

teaching.text: The calculation uses operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Its output is a **probability distribution** over possible next words.
children: The symbol **x** refers to an input, while **w** refers to a weight. They have different jobs even though both are numbers used in the calculation.
The large number of weights counts how many learned numbers the model has. It is different from the number of entries in one word vector and from the number of possible output words.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: **Synapses** are connections between neurons in the brain. Knowledge of language involves an enormous network of these connections.
children: Knowing that chickens cackle and ducks quack depends on knowledge held in the brain’s connections. A large number of connections is therefore an important feature of the human system being studied.
The approximate **150 trillion** is a count of synapses. It describes the scale of the connection network, rather than the number of words or an individual connection’s strength.

teaching.text: The scale comparison concerns the **large number of connections or weights** in each system. A large number of weights in AI is not, by itself, a reason to dismiss a connection with human knowledge.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: **Prediction** means using available information to anticipate a missing or upcoming part. In a sequence-completion task, predicting the continuation and completing the sequence describe the same task.
Treating knowledge as successful prediction is a proposal about what it means for an AI system to know something. It focuses attention on whether the system can produce an appropriate continuation.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: **Learning from mistakes** means using the difference between a prediction and the appropriate answer to improve the system. Making a prediction provides something that can be checked and corrected.
**Stochastic gradient descent, or SGD**, is a learning algorithm. A simple averaging problem makes its correction process easier to understand without requiring a complicated AI system.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: **Observation-based error learning** starts with an estimate and improves it using individual observations. In the averaging example, the estimate is a guess about the average of a list of numbers.
children: Compare the estimate with one number from the list, then move the estimate partway toward that number. Repeating this with more observations allows the data to shape the estimate.

teaching.text: The important idea is **improvement through repeated corrections**. The estimate is learned from data instead of being obtained by directly adding the whole list and dividing.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent, or SGD,** begins with an estimate **x** and compares it with a randomly selected observation **d**. The bracketed index identifies the step. **x[0] = 130** is the initial guess, and **d[0] = 98** is the observation selected for that correction.
The **loss** in this example is the signed difference between the estimate and the observation. The difference is positive because the guess is too high.
children: Subtracting a fraction of this difference lowers the estimate. If the observation were above the estimate, the difference would be negative and the same subtraction rule would raise the estimate.

teaching.text: The **10% learning rate** specifies the fraction of the gap used for the correction. **x[1] = 126.8** is the estimate after one update. It moves toward 98 without being replaced by 98.

**Stochastic** refers to random observation selection, **gradient** concerns the loss-related direction and **descent** concerns reducing the error. Repeated observations guide the estimate toward the average.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: The vertical axis **x** is the estimate, and **Epochs** marks the progress of learning along the horizontal axis. **IC** means initial condition, the estimate at the start.
children: Red begins at **130**, green at **80** and blue at **10**. Those numbers identify different starting guesses. The curves approach the same region near the average.

teaching.text: The four panels change the **learning rate**, the fraction of each discrepancy used in an update. The 1% and 10% panels make smaller corrections than the 50% and 80% panels.
children: At **1%**, the approach is slow and smooth. At **10%**, the curves reach the region sooner with modest fluctuations. At **50% and 80%**, the approach is fast, but individual observations produce much wider fluctuations.

teaching.text: The comparison separates **starting point** from **update size**. Within a panel, the colors change the starting estimate. Across panels, the learning rate changes how strongly each observation moves it.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: The **speed–accuracy tradeoff** concerns how quickly an estimate improves and how precisely it settles near the average.
children: The symbol **γ** is the learning rate. An upward arrow means increasing that quantity, and a downward arrow means decreasing it. The arrows compare settings rather than describing the direction in which the estimate must move.
A higher **learning rate**, written **γ**, gives observations more influence. The estimate changes quickly but continues to fluctuate more.
A lower learning rate makes each correction smaller. Learning is slower, but the estimate can remain closer to the average.

The graphs plot estimate **x** against learning progress, labeled **Epochs**. Comparing the 1%, 10%, 50% and 80% panels shows how a larger correction fraction gives a faster approach but wider variation near the average.

teaching.text: Improving an optimization method means trying to obtain both faster learning and greater accuracy. Changing the learning rate alone creates a tradeoff between those goals in these examples.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: A **dynamical system** can be understood through its **elements**, the **relations** between them and its **goal**. The elements are the parts, and the relations describe how those parts affect one another.
children: The goal identifies what the organized activity accomplishes. Describing the parts alone misses how their interactions produce the behavior of the whole system.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: An octopus keeping its den uses its **eight arms**, the ground and its interactions with a fish as parts of an organized action. Its nervous system is distributed through its head and body.
The **relations** between the arms, ground and fish determine how the movements work together. Their shared **goal** is to keep the den.
children: Understanding the action requires explaining the coordination between parts, rather than treating each arm movement separately.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: **Speech is a dynamical system** because several parts work together over time to convey a thought. Its elements include the tongue, lips, velum, larynx, palate and **pharyngeal wall**, the back wall of the throat.
children: The brain coordinates the relations between these parts. Producing speech depends on how their movements fit together, rather than on one structure acting alone.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: **Dynamical systems** occur throughout the body. Voluntary actions and involuntary activity in the heart, pancreas and neurons all involve parts affecting one another over time.
The elements can be whole organs, parts of organs, cells or chemicals within cells. A system can therefore be studied at different physical scales.
children: Systems with very different elements can share patterns of organization. Recognizing those shared relations helps explain behavior across biology, chemistry and physics.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: A complex octopus action can be analyzed into **motor primitives**, simpler movement components that combine to produce the full action. The slapping action involves coordinated changes in arm movement.
children: Components can combine in sequence and at the same time. Their organization helps explain how a flexible body produces a controlled action in relation to a moving fish.

teaching.text: The important question is how the movement components fit together to achieve the animal’s goal. A description of the separate parts alone does not explain the complete action.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI models psychological abilities** including knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. These abilities provide specific questions about what an artificial system can do.
In a **cloze task**, supplying a missing word tests knowledge through successful completion. This is one way to connect a psychological ability with an observable response.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: A word enters GPT as a **vector**, a list of numbers used to represent it. The inputs are written **x**, and the word representations are called **tokens**.
children: The separate vertical strips represent the input vectors for the supplied words. Each contains many numbers describing one token. They are different from the entries in the long output vector, which assign probabilities to possible next words.

teaching.text: The system combines the inputs with its **weights**, written **W**. These weights are numbers that hold learned knowledge and affect how the inputs are processed.
children: The calculations produce a **probability distribution** over possible next words. A high probability means the system strongly predicts that continuation.
The output labels “a,” “cat,” “quack” and “Zulu” identify candidate words. They are examples of entries in the distribution, not four dimensions of each input-word vector.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: **Weights begin with random values.** These starting numbers allow the system to make a prediction, but they do not yet encode useful knowledge of the language.
A training sequence provides the answer against which to check the prediction. For “chickens cackle and ducks,” the target continuation is “quack.”
children: The word **quack** identifies the training target for this sequence. Its position in the output distribution is the probability entry that should become more strongly supported. The input words remain “chickens cackle and ducks.”
The weights are changed so the output assigns more appropriate probabilities. Repeating prediction and correction across many sequences builds the system’s learned knowledge.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: **Random initialization** gives the system its starting weights. **Learning from mistakes** changes those weights after its predictions are compared with appropriate answers.
children: Starting with random weights and improving them are different steps. Random values give learning a starting point, while corrections make the values useful for prediction.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: An average can be learned by **observation-based error learning**. Start with an estimate, compare it with one observation and move it partway toward that observation.
children: Each correction uses data to improve the estimate. The procedure repeats across observations instead of calculating the average directly from the full list.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: The **estimate x** is the current guess about the average. **x[0] = 130** identifies the starting estimate, before any updates. The bracketed zero counts the step; it is not part of the guessed value.

The data list contains the observations used for learning. Their average is **80.25**, identified in the green legend as the target. The red point at 130 is a guess about that average, not the average itself.
children: The vertical axis measures the estimate, and the horizontal **Update** axis counts corrections. At update zero, no correction has yet been made.

teaching.text: The **learning rate γ = 25%** means each correction uses one quarter of the gap between the estimate and the selected observation. It controls the size of the change, rather than setting the target average.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: The current estimate is **x[0] = 130**, and the selected observation is **d[0] = 98**. The index zero identifies this comparison before the first correction.
The red point marks the estimate and the blue point marks the observation. Their vertical separation represents the **discrepancy**, called the **loss** here.
children: The difference is **32** because the estimate is above the observation. This is a signed difference, so its positive sign indicates that the estimate should decrease.

teaching.text: The vertical axis measures the numerical values, and **Update** counts corrections on the horizontal axis. The target average **80.25** refers to the whole data set. It differs from the single observation 98 used for this comparison.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: The **25% learning rate** is written as **0.25** in the correction rule. It means using one quarter of the discrepancy, not replacing the estimate with the selected observation.
The estimate starts at **130**, the selected observation is **98**, and **32** is the gap between them. Subtracting part of that positive gap produces **x[1] = 122**, the estimate after one update.
children: The red point moves down from update zero to update one. The vertical axis measures **x**, while the horizontal axis counts updates. The green line at **80.25** is the full-data average, not the observation used in this correction.

teaching.text: **The update moves toward 98 and stops short of it.** The learning rate controls how much of the gap is removed.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: The estimate entering this correction is **x[1] = 122**. The selected observation **d[1] = 85** is lower, so the positive gap calls for a downward update.
children: **x[2] = 112.75** is the estimate after two updates. The bracketed numbers count steps; they do not change the meaning of x as the estimate.

teaching.text: The **0.25** factor removes one quarter of the discrepancy. The red curve shows the resulting estimates against update number, while the green line at **80.25** identifies the average of all the data.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: The selected observation is **d[2] = 76**, below the estimate **112.75**. Their positive discrepancy is **36.75**, which tells the correction to lower the estimate.
children: The **25% learning rate** uses only one quarter of this gap. **x[3]** labels the result after three updates, rather than the selected observation.

teaching.text: The red path plots estimate **x** vertically against **Update** horizontally. Its movement is toward the selected datum, while the green **80.25** line marks the average of the complete data set.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[3] = 68** is lower than the estimate **103.563**. The difference is positive, so subtracting part of it lowers the estimate.
children: The **0.25** factor is the learning rate. At a fixed rate, a larger gap produces a larger correction. **x[4]** is the estimate after four updates.

teaching.text: The red curve records estimates on the vertical **x** axis as update number increases horizontally. The green line at **80.25** marks the full-data average, which differs from the individual observation 68.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: The selected datum **d[4] = 98** is above the current estimate **94.672**. Estimate minus observation therefore gives the negative discrepancy **−3.328**.
Subtracting one quarter of this negative difference **raises the estimate**. **x[5] = 95.504** names the result after five updates.
children: The red curve’s small upward step moves toward the selected observation. It does not mean that the average has changed. The green line at **80.25** is the fixed full-data average, and the horizontal **Update** axis counts corrections.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[5] = 72** is below the current estimate **95.504**. Their positive discrepancy calls for a decrease.
children: The **0.25** learning-rate factor uses one quarter of this gap. **x[6]** is the result after six corrections; d labels the observation and x labels the changing estimate.

teaching.text: The red curve plots those estimates against update number. The green **80.25** line is the whole-data average. An individual update moves toward its selected observation, so the path can change direction as different observations are selected.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: The current estimate **89.628** exceeds the selected observation **d[6] = 78**. The **11.628** discrepancy is the signed gap being corrected.
children: Using the **25% learning rate** lowers the estimate partway toward 78. **x[7]** identifies the estimate after seven updates.

teaching.text: The red path shows the numerical estimate on the vertical axis and its update number on the horizontal axis. The green line at **80.25** is the average of the full data set. The observation used for this correction is below that average.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[7] = 67** is lower than the estimate **86.721**, so the correction moves down. The **0.25** factor uses one quarter of the positive discrepancy.
children: **x[8]** is the result after eight updates. It is a revised estimate of the average, rather than a new observation.

teaching.text: The red estimate approaches the green **80.25** average line. The horizontal axis counts updates and the vertical axis measures x. The algorithm responds to one selected observation at a time, rather than being directly given that full-data average.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[8] = 98** is above the current estimate **81.791**. The signed difference is therefore negative, **−16.209**.
Subtracting a quarter of this negative difference increases the estimate to **x[9] = 85.843**. The red rise at update nine is the expected response to an observation above the estimate.
children: The green **80.25** line is the average of the complete data set. This one observation can pull the estimate away from that average even while the correction moves it closer to the selected datum. Individual steps can fluctuate around the overall tendency.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[9] = 85** is close to the estimate **85.843**. Their discrepancy **0.843** is small, so using one quarter of it produces a small downward correction.
children: **x[10] = 85.632** means the estimate after ten updates. The learning rate stays at **25%**; the short step comes from the small gap, rather than from a smaller rate.

teaching.text: The red estimate is almost flat between updates nine and ten. The green line at **80.25** marks the whole-data average. The vertical axis measures x and the horizontal axis counts the corrections.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: The observation **d[10] = 76** is below the current estimate **85.632**. The positive difference tells **SGD** to lower its estimate.
children: **x[11]** names the result after eleven updates. The **0.25** factor means removing one quarter of the gap, so the estimate moves partway toward 76.

teaching.text: The red path records the updated estimate x against update number, and the green **80.25** line marks the average. Rises and falls respond to different selected observations; they do not require changing the learning rule.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: The selected observation **d[11] = 68** is below the current estimate **83.224**, so the update moves down. The **25% learning rate** uses a quarter of their difference.
The result **x[12] = 79.418** is the estimate after twelve updates. It falls slightly below the green **80.25** line, which is the average of the full data set.
children: The red curve plots estimates, not observations, against update number. Being near the average shows the combined effect of partial corrections from individual observations. The algorithm has not directly calculated the full-list average.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** improves an initial estimate through repeated corrections based on randomly selected observations.
children: **Stochastic** means random observation selection. **Gradient** concerns the direction of correction related to the loss. **Descent** refers to reducing the mistake.

teaching.text: The graph plots estimate **x** vertically against **Update** horizontally. The red curve begins at **130**, the initial guess, and approaches the region of **80.25**, the average marked by the green line.
children: The path **jitters**, meaning it changes in both directions. Each selected datum can lie above or below the estimate. The overall tendency is toward the average, even though individual steps can move away from it.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: The upper graph plots the estimate **x** against **Update**, the number of corrections. Red begins at **x[0] = 140** and approaches the green target **80**, the average of the listed data.

In the update rule, **x[t]** is the estimate at step t and **x[t+1]** is the estimate after one more correction. The **0.25** learning-rate factor removes a quarter of the difference between the estimate and 80. This curve shows the mean motion toward the average.

The lower graph plots **loss L** against the same update count. **x − 80** is the signed difference from the target; squaring it makes the loss nonnegative on either side of the target. The **½** is a fixed scaling factor, not a learning rate.
children: The red estimate falls toward 80 while the blue loss falls toward **zero**, meaning no remaining distance from the target. The two vertical axes measure different quantities.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: The upper graph plots estimate **x** against update count. Red starts at **x[0] = −100**, below the green target **80**. The negative sign is part of the starting value; the bracketed zero identifies the initial step.
The data and **γ = 25% learning rate** are held fixed. Only the **initial condition** changes. Because the estimate is below the target, moving toward the target requires the estimate to rise.
The lower blue curve is **loss**, half the squared difference between x and 80. Its target is **zero**, rather than 80.
children: The numerical estimate rises while its distance from the target shrinks. A rising estimate and a falling loss are therefore consistent. The graphs have the same update axis but different vertical quantities.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: The **initial condition, IC**, is the starting estimate. Red starts at **130**, green at **80** and blue at **10**. These are three starting guesses about the same average, not three different target averages.
Each graph puts estimate **x** on the vertical axis and learning progress, labeled **Epochs**, on the horizontal axis. The panel headings change the **learning rate**.
children: **1%** uses a small fraction of each discrepancy, so the approach is slow and smooth. **10%** gives a faster approach with modest variation. **50% and 80%** react strongly to individual observations and fluctuate much more near the average.

teaching.text: Compare the colors within one panel to see the effect of the starting guess. Compare panels to see the effect of the correction fraction. The starting estimate and the learning rate are different properties of the learning process.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: The **learning tradeoff** is between speed and accuracy. A larger **learning rate γ** produces bigger corrections, so learning is faster but the estimate fluctuates more around the average.
children: The arrows beside **γ**, speed and accuracy mean increases or decreases. They compare learning settings, rather than showing whether estimate x rises or falls. In the graphs, the vertical axis is x and the horizontal **Epochs** axis marks learning progress.
A smaller learning rate produces smaller corrections. Reaching the average takes longer, but the estimate stays closer to it.

The 1%, 10%, 50% and 80% headings specify the fraction of the discrepancy used per correction. Wider fluctuations in the higher-rate panels show why a faster approach does not guarantee a more precise estimate near the average.

teaching.text: Developing better **optimization** methods means trying to improve both speed and accuracy. Simply increasing or decreasing the rate has opposing effects on those two goals in this example.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: The **shortest path problem** asks for the route with the lowest total cost from **A**, the starting state, to **J**, the destination. The letters name **states**, and each column is a stage of possible choices.
The **arrows** show the allowed direction of travel. The number beside an arrow is the cost of that one transition.
children: The **12** beside A to B means that step costs 12; **7** beside A to C is the cost of that alternative. Neither number is the complete cost of reaching J.

teaching.text: A route’s **total cost** adds the arrow costs along the whole path. Choosing the cheaper first arrow does not establish which complete route is best.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: A **greedy algorithm** chooses the lowest immediate arrow cost from its current state. At **A**, it chooses the arrow to **C** costing **7**, rather than the arrow to B costing **12**.
The numbers beside the arrows are **single-step costs**. Greedy choice repeats the same local comparison at each stage, without including the remaining cost of reaching **J**.
children: A cheap immediate step can lead to an expensive continuation. The lowest next cost and the lowest whole-route cost are different quantities.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: An **exhaustive algorithm** checks every possible route and compares their total costs. Checking all possibilities allows it to identify the lowest-cost complete route.
children: Each candidate is a complete arrow sequence from **A to J**. Its cost adds the numbers beside every arrow it uses. The letters identify intermediate states, not costs.
The number of routes grows as more stages and states are added. Exhaustive search can therefore take a very long time, even though it finds the correct answer.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: A state’s **value V** is the lowest total cost from that state to the destination **J**. The subscripts name the endpoints. **V_BJ** is the best remaining cost from B to J; **V_CJ** is the best remaining cost from C to J.
To find **V_AJ**, compare the alternatives **12 + V_BJ** and **7 + V_CJ**.
children: **12** is the cost of moving from A to B. Adding V_BJ includes the best continuation from B. **7** is the cost from A to C, and V_CJ supplies that route’s continuation.

teaching.text: The symbol **min** means choose the smaller of these complete totals. The first arrow alone is insufficient because each choice also commits to a remaining route.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: The unknown **V_BJ** and **V_CJ** are the best costs from B and C to destination J. They are **subproblems** within finding **V_AJ**, the best cost from A to J.
children: This is **Bellman’s decomposition**. Break the full problem into smaller problems whose solutions provide the information required by the larger problem.

The **12** and **7** are already known immediate costs from A. What is missing is the best cost of each continuation. Solving those smaller problems supplies the information needed for the min comparison.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: The destination is **J**. The last states connect directly to it, so **V_GJ = 5**, **V_HJ = 9** and **V_IJ = 8** are known from their final arrows.
children: These are complete remaining costs because each route has only its final transition left.

teaching.text: A value farther from J combines an **immediate arrow cost** with a **remaining value**. In **8 + V_GJ**, 8 is the cost from D to G and V_GJ is the best cost from G to J.
children: The **min** chooses the smallest combined total among the possible next states. This supplies a value for D, E or F, which can then be used to solve the values of B and C.

teaching.text: The red curved arrows beside the equations show known values being used in the problems that depend on them. Value calculation proceeds from the destination toward the start, opposite the direction in which the final route is traveled.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: A **value** includes the best remaining cost to **J**. A raw arrow number includes only one transition. Calculate the values before choosing the complete route.
At **A**, compare **12 + V_BJ** with **7 + V_CJ**. The immediate cost must be included even when the remaining values are known.
children: The **min** operation selects the smaller combined cost. The same comparison selects the next step at each state until reaching J.

teaching.text: The red dependency arrows beside the equations trace the reuse of computed values. The route through the state network follows the black travel arrows from A toward J. The two sets of arrows have different jobs.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: A **state value** summarizes the best total cost from that state to the destination. A costly obstacle near the end of a route therefore affects values calculated at earlier states.
children: This prevents an inexpensive initial arrow from appearing attractive when its continuation is expensive.

The **9** beside H to J is the cost of that final transition. Its effect is included in the values of routes that lead through H. A value therefore accounts for a late cost before a starting choice is made.

teaching.text: The values are calculated **backward** from the destination. The route is then followed **forward** from the start, using the stored values to select each step.
children: The red curved arrows beside the equations show information being used to calculate values in preceding stages. The black arrows in the state network show allowed travel from **A to J**.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming decomposes a problem into smaller subproblems.** If a subproblem still depends on unknown information, it is broken into smaller problems in turn.
children: The process reaches cases simple enough to solve directly. Their answers are then used to solve the larger problems that depend on them.

teaching.text: The full solution is built from these smaller solutions. A solved subproblem supplies an answer that can be reused wherever it is needed.
children: The subscripted **V** terms refer to best costs between named states. The **min** selects the smallest candidate, and each candidate adds one arrow’s cost to a known continuation value. The red arrows show how a solved value supplies an input to another calculation.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: **Bellman’s rule** compares complete continuations from a state. The notation **V_DJ** means the best remaining cost from D to destination J.
For D, the candidate **8 + V_GJ** combines the cost of the arrow from D to G with the best remaining cost from G to J. The other candidates do the same for routes through H and I.
children: **min** means keep the smallest of those totals. The numbers outside the V terms are immediate arrow costs, while the V terms are remaining-route costs.

teaching.text: The known final values **5, 9 and 8** correspond to G, H and I. The red arrows trace those values into the larger subproblems that use them. Reusing each solution avoids checking the same continuation repeatedly.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: The **lowest total cost** can require choosing a more expensive initial step. That step can lead to a cheaper continuation and avoid a large cost near the end.
children: The network’s **12** is an early arrow cost, while the **9** near the end is a later transition cost. Accepting the larger immediate cost can lead to a route with a smaller total.

teaching.text: The **shortest distance** and **least time** are also different goals. When movement has the same speed everywhere, a straight route is fastest. When running on sand is faster than swimming, spending more of the route on sand can reduce the total time.
children: The beach diagrams compare **one speed throughout** with **different speeds on sand and in water**. The bend in the least-time route lets more travel occur where movement is faster.
The best route depends on what is being minimized and on the costs of all its parts.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes between media in which its speed differs. The route taken is a **least-time path**.
children: The fastest complete route can include different distances in the two media. Minimizing travel time is therefore different from requiring the shortest straight-line distance.

The media are labeled **Air (Faster Light)** and **Water (Slower Light)**. The bent light path changes how much distance is traveled in each medium. The pencil’s apparent bend illustrates the resulting refraction.

teaching.text: An optimization problem must account for the **total cost across the route**. In the network, a more expensive early arrow can be worthwhile if it avoids a greater cost in the continuation.
children: The route diagrams distinguish a straight **shortest-distance path** from a bent **least-time path** when speeds differ. The network numbers, including **12** and **9**, are costs attached to parts of a route, so the complete comparison must include the continuation.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: The small numbers beside arrows are **immediate transition costs**. The blue handwritten annotations at states combine a **best remaining cost** with the **next state to choose**.
children: **30 B** at A means the best total cost from A to J is 30 and the route should next go to B. It does not say that the A-to-B arrow itself costs 30.

teaching.text: Following the chosen-state annotations gives **A → B → D → G → J**. For example, **18 D** at B means a best remaining cost of 18 through D; **13 G** at D points to G; **5 J** at G identifies the final step.

The route is selected using each **arrow cost plus the value at its destination**. The start can therefore choose the arrow costing **12** to B even though the arrow costing **7** to C is immediately cheaper. The annotations describe the lowest complete route cost.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: The learning graph plots **estimate x** vertically against learning progress, labeled **Epochs**, horizontally. **IC** means initial condition: red starts at **130**, green at **80** and blue at **10**.
children: The curves approach the region near the average. The **10% learning rate** is the fraction of each discrepancy used to correct the estimate; it is not a target value.

teaching.text: The temperature graph plots **temperature in degrees Celsius** against **minutes**. Hot coffee starts above room temperature and cools, while iced coffee starts below it and warms.
children: The dashed **18°C** line is room temperature, the common equilibrium level. The different black curves begin at different temperatures rather than having different room-temperature targets.

teaching.text: Both graphs show an **approach to equilibrium**. Change is fast when the system is far from the stable level and slower near it. The horizontal axes measure different kinds of progress, and the vertical axes measure different quantities.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** has two quantities that change together. **Position, x,** tells where something is relative to its resting position. **Velocity, v,** tells how its position is changing.
children: A dot above a letter means its **rate of change**. The symbol ẋ is the rate of change of position, while v̇ is the rate of change of velocity.

teaching.text: The rule **ẋ = v** says that velocity determines how position changes. Positive velocity makes position increase, and negative velocity makes it decrease.
The rule **v̇ = −x** says that position changes velocity with the sign reversed. Positive position makes velocity decrease, while negative position makes velocity increase.
children: The minus sign gives the opposing direction of this effect. Position and velocity keep changing one another through this loop.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: **Velocity, v,** determines the direction in which **position, x,** changes. In the example **v = −5**, the negative sign means position decreases.
children: This describes the direction of motion. It does not say that the current position itself must be negative.

teaching.text: In the example **x = −5**, position is on the negative side of equilibrium. The rule **v̇ = −x** then makes the change in velocity positive.
children: Velocity rises because the rule reverses the sign of position. It can become less negative before it becomes positive, so rising velocity does not always mean speeding up in the current direction.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: The rule **ẋ = v** connects velocity to changing position. If **v** is positive, **x** rises. If v is negative, x falls.
children: The dot belongs to the rate of change, so positive ẋ means position is increasing rather than saying where the object currently is.

teaching.text: The rule **v̇ = −x** connects position to changing velocity. If x is positive, **v** falls. If x is negative, v rises.
children: An object can be on the positive side while moving toward smaller positions. Its position, velocity, and change in velocity describe different aspects of its motion.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: Suppose **position is negative and velocity is zero**. Negative position makes velocity rise above zero, and that positive velocity moves the object toward the resting position.
children: The object still has positive velocity when it reaches the resting position, so it continues into positive positions.

teaching.text: Once position is positive, velocity begins to fall. It reaches zero and then becomes negative, turning the motion back toward the other side.
children: This continuing change between position and velocity produces an **oscillation**, or repeated back-and-forth motion.

teaching.text: The position and velocity curves do not reach their peaks together. **Velocity is zero at a turning point**, but it can be large when position passes through zero.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: The arrows between **position, x, and velocity, v,** form a **feedback loop**. Position changes velocity, and velocity changes position.
children: The effect returns to the quantity that started it, so the interaction continues. This repeated interaction produces the back-and-forth change called **oscillation** or **vibration**.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** describes a repeating pattern of change. The same basic idea is useful for studying vibrations in different physical systems.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: During **compression**, air particles move closer together and pressure becomes higher. During **rarefaction**, they move farther apart and pressure becomes lower.
children: The particles stay the same size. What changes is the space between them.

teaching.text: The dashed boundary marks the slice’s **equilibrium size**. The highlighted pair makes its changing distance visible.
children: **100%** means the pair is at its equilibrium spacing. A percentage below 100% means the particles are closer together, while a percentage above 100% means they are farther apart.

teaching.text: The slice repeatedly contracts and expands through these states. The percentages describe relative spacing rather than the percentage of particles present.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: A **cosine** describes the repeating expansion and compression of the air slice. **x** is a scaled measure of expansion.
children: **+1** means maximum rarefaction, with the particles farthest apart. **0** means equilibrium spacing. **−1** means maximum compression, with the particles closest together. These are relative values rather than distances in centimeters.

teaching.text: The horizontal axis shows **phase**, meaning how far the motion has progressed through its repeating cycle. The marks are phase values rather than seconds.
children: From **0 to 2π** is one complete cycle. At 0 the air is maximally expanded, at **π** it is maximally compressed, and at 2π it is maximally expanded again. The range to **6π** contains three cycles.

teaching.text: The moving point connects a value on the curve with the air spacing at that moment. The curve shows changing expansion rather than the path followed by individual particles.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: **Tongue height** describes how high or low the tongue is. **Tongue backness** describes how far toward the front or back its raised region lies.
children: The vowels in **dean** and **dune** are both high. Dean is front, while dune is back.
The vowels in **Dan** and **Don** are low in this comparison. Dan is front, Don is back, and **done** is central.

teaching.text: These different tongue positions change the shape of the **vocal tract**, the air space above the vocal folds. The air has less room in some places and more room in others.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration

teaching.text: A vowel can combine **more than one frequency**. Each component is a repeating vibration, and adding the components produces a more complex pattern.
children: The illustrative **/i/** model combines **1 Hz and 4 Hz**. The illustrative **/a/** model combines **2 Hz and 3 Hz**. **Hertz, Hz,** means cycles per second. These deliberately slow values make the patterns visible.

teaching.text: In the graphs, **t** is signal time in seconds, and **x(t)** is the combined expansion at that time. Each cosine term contributes one component vibration.
children: The **vertical axis is scaled from −2 to +2** for the sum of two component waves. Positive values show rarefaction, zero shows equilibrium spacing, and negative values show compression.
The multiplying factors inside the cosine terms set the components’ repetition rates. They are not measurements of the air’s pressure or spacing.

teaching.text: Both combinations begin at the same expanded state and return to it once per second, but their motion within that second differs.
children: Which frequencies are combined determines the detailed pattern. These are visible models rather than measured frequencies of human vowels.

sections.title: Praat demonstration
Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: Speech involves two physically different kinds of vibration. The **vocal folds** are tissue that opens and closes. The **air in the vocal tract** vibrates through changing compression and rarefaction.
children: The vocal folds provide the sound source that sets the air into vibration. Explaining the moving folds and explaining the moving air are separate parts of understanding speech.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: The **business cycle** is a repeating rise and fall in economic output. Output rises during recovery, reaches a **peak**, falls during recession, and reaches a **trough** before rising again.
children: Time runs horizontally, while the level of output runs vertically.

teaching.text: The long-term **growth trend** rises even while the cycle moves above and below it. Repeated fluctuation can therefore occur around a baseline that is itself changing.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Musical sound depends on vibration.** A repeating physical motion produces the changing sound pressure that makes a musical tone.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: The magnesium example compares a historical shell picture with a **quantum orbital** picture. **Mg** names magnesium, and neutral magnesium has **12 electrons**.
children: The shell arrangement **2–8–2** counts the electrons assigned to the first, second, and third shells. It does not give vibration frequencies.

teaching.text: The orbital picture describes **electron density**, with darker regions representing greater density rather than a tiny particle travelling on a fixed circular path.
children: **1s, 2s, 2p, and 3s** name the occupied orbital groups. The raised numbers in **1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²** count the electrons contributing from those groups.

teaching.text: The total-density picture combines those occupied-group contributions. The separate thumbnails use their own scales, so their drawn sizes are not a shared distance measurement.
children: These **wave modes** are allowed quantum patterns. The use of wave patterns does not make magnesium a simple classical harmonic oscillator.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration
Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: **Position, x,** tells where something is relative to its resting position. **Velocity, v,** tells how that position changes. A dot over either letter means its **rate of change with time**.
In **ẋ = v**, velocity determines the change in position. Positive v makes x rise, while negative v makes x fall.
In **v̇ = −x**, position determines the change in velocity with the sign reversed. Positive x makes v fall, while negative x makes v rise.
children: The two arrows connect these effects into a **feedback loop**. The dot distinguishes a change from the quantity being changed.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: **Oscillation**, or **vibration**, is repeated back-and-forth change. The arrows from position to velocity and back to position make a closed **feedback loop**.
children: A change in either quantity affects the other, which returns to affect the first. The repetition comes from this continuing interaction.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: A **spring** pulls a displaced system toward its resting position. **Stiffness** tells how strongly the spring pushes back for a given displacement.
**Mass** supplies the tendency to continue moving. The spring can bring a moving mass toward the resting position, but reaching that position does not automatically stop it.
children: The mass passes through the resting position. The spring then acts from the other side and turns it back. **Spring action and continued motion together produce vibration.**

teaching.text: Both **vocal-fold tissue** and **air in the vocal tract** vibrate during speech. Understanding the returning action and the moving material helps explain those vibrations.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: **Compression** brings air particles closer together and raises pressure. **Rarefaction** spreads them farther apart and lowers pressure.
children: The same particles remain present and keep the same size. Their spacing changes as the air slice contracts and expands.

teaching.text: The dashed boundary marks the **equilibrium size**, and the highlighted pair tracks the spacing between particles.
children: **100%** is that pair’s equilibrium distance. A smaller percentage means compression, while a larger percentage means rarefaction. It is a comparison with the resting spacing, not a count of particles.

teaching.text: Compressed air pushes back, and moving air has mass. Those returning and continuing effects provide the ingredients for vibration.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: **Negative feedback**, also called **balancing feedback**, reduces displacement from **equilibrium**, the resting position at **x = 0**. Here x means displacement, and **ẋ** means its rate of change.
children: In **ẋ = −⅓x**, the minus sign makes the change oppose the displacement. Positive x gives a negative rate and x falls. Negative x gives a positive rate and x rises.

teaching.text: The **one-third coefficient** sets the strength of the returning effect in this model. Its size determines how strongly the current displacement affects the rate of change.
children: The starting value **x = 1** is an **initial condition**, the position from which the return begins. As the displacement shrinks, the return-driving rate becomes smaller too.

teaching.text: The vertical axis shows **x**, and the horizontal **t** axis shows time. A curve approaching zero steeply and then flattening means a fast initial return that gradually slows.
children: A larger returning coefficient makes the approach faster. The negative sign supplies the direction; the coefficient’s magnitude supplies the strength.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: **Inertia** is the tendency of a mass to continue its motion unless something changes that motion. The arrow in the demonstration shows the direction of **constant velocity**.
children: Constant velocity means travelling the same distance during each equal time interval. The position changes even though velocity stays the same.

teaching.text: A moving mass does not stop simply because it reaches a particular place. This is why a mass moving toward equilibrium can pass through it.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: **Displacement, x,** measures distance and direction from the spring’s natural position. **x = 0** is equilibrium, **x = +1** is the stretched-side example, and **x = −1** is the compressed-side example.
children: The signs identify opposite sides of the same resting position. They do not tell whether the endpoint is currently moving toward or away from equilibrium.

teaching.text: In the spring-only model, the endpoint approaches zero without repeatedly crossing it. The blue and red traces begin on opposite sides and approach the same resting position.
Attaching a **mass** changes the motion. The spring brings the mass toward equilibrium, but the mass continues through it because it is already moving.
children: The spring then acts from the other side and turns the mass back. The oscillating trace crosses zero repeatedly, while its peaks become smaller.

teaching.text: The trace’s vertical value is displacement and its horizontal direction follows time. A zero crossing is a moment at the resting position; a peak or trough is a turning point in the motion.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: The **cosine** curve follows the expansion and compression of the air slice. **x** is a relative measure of expansion rather than a physical distance or a pressure reading.
children: **+1** means maximum rarefaction, **0** means equilibrium spacing, and **−1** means maximum compression.

teaching.text: The horizontal axis shows **phase**, how far the vibration has progressed through its repeating cycle. From **0 to 2π** is one cycle, not two seconds.
children: The motion starts maximally expanded at 0, becomes maximally compressed at **π**, and returns to maximum expansion at 2π. The range through **6π** shows three cycles.

teaching.text: The moving point connects the graph with the particle spacing at that stage. The air particles do not travel along the wavy shape of the curve.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: **Vowel height** describes how high the tongue is, while **backness** describes how far forward or back its raised region lies.
children: The vowels in dean and dune are both high. Dean is front, and dune is back.
Dan is low and front, Don is low and back in this comparison, and done is central.

teaching.text: Moving the tongue changes where the **vocal tract** is narrow or wide. Changing that air space changes the way the air can vibrate.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval

teaching.text: **Frequency** describes how many complete cycles occur in a given time. The three panels all cover the **same 0–12-second interval**.
children: The low-frequency example completes **3 cycles**, the middle one completes **6**, and the high one completes **9**. Those numbers count cycles over twelve seconds; they are not labels saying 3, 6, or 9 cycles per second.

teaching.text: Time runs along each horizontal axis. The vertical **x** value measures relative expansion, with **+1** for maximum rarefaction, **0** for equilibrium spacing, and **−1** for maximum compression.
The spacing range is the same in all three panels. **The extent of expansion and the frequency are different properties.** More cycles fit into the same time when the motion repeats faster.

sections.title: Different combinations give different vowel patterns

teaching.text: The illustrative **/i/** and **/a/** models combine different frequency components. The /i/ model uses **1 Hz and 4 Hz**, while the /a/ model uses **2 Hz and 3 Hz**.
children: **Hertz, Hz,** means cycles per second. The slow frequencies allow the combined movement to be seen rather than giving measured human vowel frequencies.

teaching.text: The horizontal **t** axis is signal time in seconds, and **x(t)** means combined expansion at that time. Each cosine contributes one component to that combined value.
children: The **vertical axis is scaled from −2 to +2** for the sum of two component waves. Positive values mean rarefaction, zero means equilibrium spacing, and negative values mean compression.
The multiplying factors inside the cosine terms set the components’ repetition rates. They are not measurements of the air’s pressure or spacing.

teaching.text: Both patterns begin at the same expanded state and repeat once per second, but their motion within each second is different.
children: Their different component frequencies create different arrangements of peaks and troughs. The moving points and particle diagrams show the resulting combined vibration.

sections.title: Predict the effect of mass and stiffness

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts how a system changes when one of its properties changes. In the notation, **m** means mass, **k** means stiffness, and **f** means frequency.
children: An upward arrow means an increase, and a downward arrow means a decrease.

teaching.text: Increasing **m**, while stiffness stays fixed, lowers **f**. A heavier mass is harder to slow and turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
children: Increasing **k**, while mass stays fixed, raises f. A stronger returning force turns the mass around sooner, so the cycle repeats faster.

teaching.text: The arrow summaries express these directions of change. They do not give a particular frequency value or require a calculation.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies

teaching.text: The **basilar membrane** has different mass and stiffness along its length. **Large M and small k** describe its heavier, less stiff end, while **small m and large K** describe its lighter, stiffer end.
children: The size distinctions describe how much mass or stiffness each region has. They do not name different kinds of material.

teaching.text: The heavier, less stiff end responds to **lower frequencies**. The lighter, stiffer end responds to **higher frequencies**.
children: Greater mass favors slower vibration, while greater stiffness favors faster vibration.

teaching.text: Neurons carry signals from different places along the membrane to the brain. **Where the vibration occurs** therefore provides information about which frequencies are present in the sound.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness

teaching.text: The **learning rate, γ**, controls the size of each correction to an estimate. In the graphs, the vertical **x** value is the current estimate, and the horizontal **Epochs** axis records the displayed count of learning updates.
children: The red, green, and blue runs start near **130, 80, and 10**. They are different starting estimates moving toward a target near **80**.

teaching.text: The panels compare learning rates of **1%, 10%, 50%, and 80%**. A larger percentage makes each update more responsive to the current observation.
children: At 1%, the runs move steadily but approach slowly. At 10%, they reach the target region sooner with small fluctuations. At 50% and 80%, they reach it quickly but continue bouncing more widely.

teaching.text: This is the **speed–accuracy tradeoff**. Reaching the target region quickly differs from remaining close to it.
children: The arrow summaries say that increasing γ raises speed but lowers steadiness or accuracy in these runs. Decreasing γ reverses that tradeoff.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 6
Exam reminder
A spring alone and a mass–spring system

teaching.text: The spring’s **equilibrium** is its natural resting position, marked **x = 0**. **x** is displacement from that position, so positive and negative values identify its two sides.
children: In the spring-only model, a stretched endpoint approaches zero from one side and a compressed endpoint approaches it from the other.

teaching.text: A **mass–spring system** also has inertia. The spring moves the mass toward equilibrium, and the mass continues through it because it is already moving.
children: The spring then acts from the other side and turns the mass back. This interaction gives repeated crossings and turns, which make an **oscillation**.

teaching.text: The traces show displacement changing with time. Reaching zero means arriving at the resting position; it does not by itself mean the moving mass has stopped.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts the effect of changing mass or stiffness. **m** means mass, **k** means stiffness, and **f** means frequency. The arrows indicate increases or decreases.
children: Increasing m lowers f when stiffness stays fixed. More mass takes longer to turn around.
Increasing k raises f when mass stays fixed. A stiffer spring provides a stronger returning action.

teaching.text: During speech, changing the shape of the **vocal tract** changes how different portions of air behave. The air can vibrate at several frequencies, and the pattern differs between speech sounds.
children: The listener’s ear separates the frequencies present in that pattern so that different speech sounds can be distinguished.

sections.title: The cochlea connects incoming sound to neural signals

teaching.text: The **cochlea** is the coiled part of the inner ear that sends the brain information about sound frequencies.
children: Sound vibrations enter through the outer ear and travel inward to the cochlea. The important connection is between incoming vibration and the neural signals used for hearing.

sections.title: The path into the basilar membrane

teaching.text: The **basilar membrane** runs along the inside of the cochlea. The membrane is coiled with it, but it can be understood as a long strip.
children: Sound vibration passes inward from the eardrum and the small connecting bones to the cochlea.

teaching.text: The membrane’s physical properties change along its length. Different parts can therefore respond most strongly to different frequencies rather than responding in exactly the same way.

sections.title: Frequency is represented by place and nerve activity

teaching.text: Different locations on the **basilar membrane** respond to different frequencies. The heavier, less stiff end responds to low frequencies. The lighter, stiffer end responds to high frequencies.
children: The mass and stiffness distinctions concern the membrane’s physical properties. **Frequency** concerns how quickly the vibration repeats.

teaching.text: The **neurons** carry signals from those locations **to the brain**. The information path runs from sound-driven vibration to activity at particular places and then to the brain.
children: Activity at different locations tells the brain which frequencies are present in the incoming sound.

sections.title: How vocal folds make and change pitch

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are small muscles with both mass and stiffness. The stated **one-centimeter length and one-millimeter height** describe their physical size.
children: Other muscles can stretch the folds to make them stiffer or bunch them to make them effectively heavier. Stiffer folds vibrate faster, while heavier folds vibrate more slowly.

teaching.text: Their vibration rate is the **fundamental frequency, F0**. The zero is part of the frequency’s name, not a claim that the folds vibrate zero times.
children: This rate is closely connected with **pitch**. Changing it allows singing and can signal questions, surprise, or emotion. In a **tone language**, pitch differences can distinguish word meanings.

teaching.text: Vibration begins when pressure builds beneath closed folds and pushes them apart. Air flows through the opening, and the airflow draws the folds inward again.
children: This inward effect is called the **Bernoulli force**. Repeated opening and closing can occur hundreds of times per second; that is a rate of vibration rather than a physical dimension.

sections.title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded

teaching.text: The oscillator tracks **position, x,** and **velocity, v**. It starts at **x = 1 and v = 0**, meaning an initial displacement with no initial motion.
children: **k** means stiffness and **m** means mass. The displayed **k/m = 1** sets their ratio for this example. **Δt**, also written **dt**, is the time step, set to **0.5** model-time units.

teaching.text: At each step, velocity is used to update position, and the **new position** is then used to update velocity.
children: The x and v lists store the successive states. The plotted decimals are rounded values of position or velocity at those sampled times, rather than new coefficients.

teaching.text: The horizontal **t** axes show time, and the vertical axes show x or v. Position passes through zero while velocity can still be nonzero. At a turning point in position, velocity is zero.
children: The plotted swings stay near their original range. Which state each update uses is part of the procedure.

sections.title: Explicit Euler uses the old pair for both updates

teaching.text: **Explicit Euler** tracks **position, x,** and **velocity, v**, with **k** for stiffness and **m** for mass. The example starts at **x[0] = 1 and v[0] = 0**, with k and m both set to 1.
children: **dt = 0.5** is the time step. The bracketed **n** counts update steps, and **n−1** identifies the preceding step. These indexes identify when a value was stored.

teaching.text: Both new values use the **previous pair**, x[n−1] and v[n−1]. The velocity update uses the old position rather than the position just computed.
children: Each list holds successive positions or velocities. The decimals beside the plotted points are rounded results for those states rather than new equation coefficients.

teaching.text: The horizontal axes show **time**, while the vertical axes separately show x and v. The swings grow larger as time advances.
children: That growing **amplitude**, or extent of the swings, comes from the numerical approximation with this time step. It does not mean an extra physical force was added to the oscillator.

sections.title: Arithmetic can approximate continuous change

teaching.text: **Euler’s explicit method** turns a rule about change into repeated arithmetic. In **x[n]**, x is the changing quantity and n identifies its update step. **x[n−1]** is its value at the previous step.
children: **dt** is the small time interval. The update adds the estimated change during that interval to the previous value.

teaching.text: Repeating this operation builds an approximate sequence of states. A computer can follow a system’s changing behavior through the same simple operation again and again.
children: The result is an **approximation**. Its accuracy depends on the time step and the way the update is performed.

Differential equations express how systems change

teaching.text: A **differential equation** describes a relationship involving a rate of change. It connects what a system is doing now with how its quantities change over time.
children: This is the mathematical form of a **dynamical system**, a system whose state develops through time.

teaching.text: Knowing a rule for change helps predict a system’s behavior from a starting state. The same broad perspective connects physical systems with learning and inference in language models.

sections.title: Predict a return toward equilibrium step by step

teaching.text: **Negative feedback**, or **balancing feedback**, makes a change oppose the current displacement. Here **x** is the changing value, **ẋ** is its rate of change, and **t** is time.
children: In **ẋ = −⅓x**, the minus sign supplies the opposing direction and one third supplies the strength of the effect. A value above zero decreases toward zero, while a value below zero increases toward zero.

teaching.text: The **initial condition** is **x = 100 at t = 0**. It identifies the starting value and starting time rather than a separate target.
children: The approximate value near **66 or 67** is a result of applying one displayed update. It is not a changed coefficient. Each update is then based on the current, smaller value.

teaching.text: The horizontal axis follows time, and the vertical axis follows x. As the discrepancy from equilibrium shrinks, the return slows and the curve flattens.
children: **Euler’s method** constructs this approximate sequence by using the previous value to estimate the next. A time subscript identifies which value in that sequence is being used.
